blocks.text: Accelerate is the Hugging Face library that handles the distributed and mixed precision training details covered conceptually in the earlier Distributed Training Techniques module, letting the same training code run unchanged on a single CPU, a single GPU, or many GPUs across multiple machines.
This topic covers how Accelerate wraps existing training code with minimal changes, how it picks a distributed backend, and how it fits underneath the other frameworks covered in this module.

Writing training code that works correctly across different hardware setups, a laptop CPU, a single GPU, multiple GPUs, or multiple machines, traditionally required different code paths for each, Accelerate abstracts these differences so the same training script runs correctly regardless of the underlying hardware.

The core API pattern wraps your existing model, optimizer, and dataloader objects through a single accelerator.prepare call, which returns versions of those same objects configured correctly for whatever distributed setup Accelerate detects, without needing separate code for each hardware configuration.

code.content:
from accelerate import Accelerator

accelerator = Accelerator()
model, optimizer, dataloader = accelerator.prepare(model, optimizer, dataloader)

for batch in dataloader:
    outputs = model(**batch)
    loss = outputs.loss
    accelerator.backward(loss)
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

blocks.text: The one notable change to a typical training loop is calling accelerator.backward instead of the usual loss.backward, this lets Accelerate correctly handle gradient scaling for mixed precision and gradient synchronization across devices behind the scenes, without the training loop needing to manage those details directly.

Before running a training script, accelerate config walks through an interactive setup asking about the target hardware, number of GPUs, mixed precision settings, saving a configuration file that accelerate launch then reads to actually start the training run correctly distributed across the configured hardware.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Command","Purpose"],"rows":[["accelerate config","Interactively define the target hardware and distributed setup"],["accelerate launch script.py","Run a training script using the saved configuration"]]}

blocks.text: Accelerate does not implement distributed training from scratch, it provides a unified interface over established backends, standard PyTorch DDP for straightforward multi-GPU training, or DeepSpeed and FSDP, both covered conceptually in the earlier Distributed Training Techniques module, for more advanced memory-saving strategies at larger scale.

Enabling mixed precision training, covered conceptually in an earlier module, is typically a single configuration flag with Accelerate, fp16 or bf16, rather than manually managing casting and gradient scaling logic throughout a training loop.

blocks.title: Accelerate handles the fiddly precision details automatically
blocks.content: Manually managing mixed precision correctly, gradient scaling, avoiding overflow, casting at the right points, is a common source of subtle bugs, Accelerate handling this centrally removes an entire category of easy mistakes.

blocks.text: 7. Where Accelerate Sits in the Framework Stack

blocks.alt: Where Accelerate Sits in the Framework Stack

blocks.text: Accelerate typically operates beneath the higher level libraries covered elsewhere in this module, the Trainer API in Transformers and the trainer classes in TRL, both covered in earlier topics, use Accelerate internally to handle their own distributed training, so many users benefit from Accelerate without calling its API directly at all.

Using the Accelerate API directly, rather than through the Trainer API, makes sense when writing a custom training loop, covered as an option in the earlier Hugging Face Transformers topic, that still needs to scale correctly across different hardware without hand-rolling distributed logic.

Accelerate provides utilities for consistent logging and checkpointing across distributed processes, avoiding a common pitfall where every process independently prints or saves output, since only the main process typically should perform these actions in a multi-process training run.

A team writes a custom training loop for a specialized fine-tuning task that the Trainer API configuration options do not directly support. To make the loop scale across their multi-GPU training server without writing separate distributed logic, they wrap the model, optimizer, and dataloader with accelerator.prepare and swap loss.backward for accelerator.backward.

Running accelerate config once to describe their four-GPU setup, then accelerate launch to start training, the same script runs correctly whether tested locally on a single GPU or launched on the full multi-GPU server, with no additional code changes required between the two.

items: Forgetting to swap loss.backward for accelerator.backward, breaking mixed precision and multi-device gradient handling
Having every distributed process independently log or save checkpoints instead of gating that behavior to the main process
Writing custom distributed logic by hand when Accelerate already handles the same problem in a tested, hardware-agnostic way
Not running accelerate config before accelerate launch, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual hardware setup

blocks.text: Take a simple single GPU training loop you are familiar with, or one from an earlier topic in this course, and identify exactly which lines would need to change to use Accelerate, the prepare call and the backward call, and explain why those specific changes are the ones that need to happen.

Accelerate lets the same training code run correctly across CPU, single GPU, or multi-GPU and multi-machine setups by wrapping the model, optimizer, and dataloader through accelerator.prepare and routing the backward pass through accelerator.backward, and it operates underneath the Trainer API and TRL trainers covered elsewhere in this module, handling distributed training details that would otherwise need to be managed by hand.
